doc.title: Bill Crow interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: Dave Lambert and the New York scuffle
summary: Dave Lambert teaches him to survive poor and introduces him to Hefti, Roland, Moondog and the jam session world; Buzzy lands a Tupper Lake job.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: ever addressed. So I got to a point with him where I couldn’t stand my day job, and decided that I couldn’t go there anymore. It was just emotionally too shattering to go into that atmosphere every day. So without my day job, then I fell behind on my payments to my therapist, and he suggested that I go out and get another job and live my life and maybe I could afford to talk to a therapist sometime in the future. So I did. I scuffled around New York. And actually I was very lucky to have fallen in with Dave Lambert and his wife and four year old daughter. They were living down in the lower East Side on a part of Monroe Street that’s no longer there now, they’ve built a project across that section of the block. But they had a twenty dollar a month apartment and they were happy as clams, and they had no income. And so they taught me how to survive. You know it doesn’t make you a bad person to be poor, and that it’s possible to still live and be productive and live kind of hand to mouth. It wasn’t that he had no income, it’s just that he didn’t know where the next dollar was going to come from. But he was a willing worker and he had a wonderful attitude toward giving people value for service, and if you couldn’t, if you had to prevail on somebody to give you a handout, at least you could entertain them. So he was always very welcome at parties. He knew a few songwriters who were willing to give us a meal, that kind of thing. So I really got my New York education from Davey. He showed me how to scuffle and he showed me who the interesting people were, whether they were making any money or not, he knew who the artists were and who the interesting characters were around town. And that was a wonderful education for me. And also through him, let’s see now, well I had already known this guy Buzzy that I came out here with. And they all introduced me to people like Neal Hefti and Gene Roland and Moondog, and Larry Rivers was a tenor player there then instead of a painter, and a whole world of jam sessions: Zoot Simms and Brew Moore and people that were just around playing wherever there was a loft or a rehearsal studio or someplace like that to play. And the first summer that I was here, Buzzy got a job with Gene Roland up in Tupper Lake, New York, you may know where that is, a place called the Altamont Hotel, it burned down later, but it was a nice old hotel and it was far enough out of the real borsht belt type of entertainment that they didn’t have a set agenda for what an entertaining band should be. So Gene had talked them into a quartet. He went up there with drums, tenor, piano, and maybe a saxophone player, I’m not sure. But anyway Buzzy was his drummer. And the first night that they were on the job they were going to go up for the summer in 1950. The first night on the job Gene has a big fight with the boss’s wife and stalks out, abandons the band. So Buzzy goes to the boss and says “look there’s no reason why you should be stuck without a band, let me go to New York and get you some guys” because he didn’t particularly like the other guys that Gene had hired.
